summary.alternatives_overview.extracted_value: The Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) compares Amistad hydropower to five other ways of producing the same electricity — natural gas, fuel oil, coal, Texas lignite, and nuclear — plus a 'no action' option of building nothing. Natural gas is rejected because it is scarce and under a moratorium on new gas-fired plants, and fuel oil because it would require imported foreign oil. High-quality coal deposits in Webb County are too small to support a mine-mouth plant, and northern coal has unresolved sulfur-oxide emissions problems: of 24 stack-gas cleaning installations at U.S. coal-fired plants of 150 MW or larger, none was in satisfactory operation in 1974. Lignite and coal plants are base-load (they run at steady output and can't efficiently follow peak demand the way hydropower can), and nuclear is not viable because projected cumulative uranium demand by 2000 (2.4 to 3.1 million tons of U3O8) far exceeds the estimated reserve base of 500,000 tons. Under 'no action,' the consumers would likely get power from imported oil or south Texas lignite instead.
summary.alternatives_overview.evidence_quote: Of 24 stack gas installations at coal-fired power plants of 150 MW or larger in the United States, none was in satisfactory operation in 1974.

summary.environmental_impact.extracted_value: During the 2-3 year construction period, impacts include temporary dust and exhaust emissions, sedimentation from a cofferdam in the streambed, and construction noise. During operation, Amistad's conservation pool would drop by an average of 2 feet while Falcon's pool would rise about 3 feet, and daily hydropower releases would raise the river roughly 4 feet just below the dam, decreasing to under 2 feet below Eagle Pass. The most significant impact is on the tailrace fishery: from roughly May through November, bottom-water released through the penstocks could be 10-12 °C colder and carry near-zero oxygen into the first 2.2 miles below the dam, possibly causing minor fish kills. Bank sloughing (bank collapse) would increase initially — observed about six miles downstream during a 9,000 cfs test release — and the Fish and Wildlife Service warned that altered flows and reservoir fluctuation 'could have a profound effect on existing fishery resources.' The plant would annually offset roughly 482,000 tons of Texas lignite, about 625,000 barrels of oil, or 3.1 billion cubic feet of natural gas, and no properties on the National Register of Historic Places would be affected.

summary.overview.extracted_value: The U.S. Section of the International Boundary and Water Commission proposes to add a 57,000 kW hydroelectric power plant (with two turbine-generator units) to the existing Amistad Dam on the Rio Grande, about 12 miles upstream of Del Rio, Texas, at a cost of about $28 million and 2-3 years of construction. The power would serve about 464,391 people across eight south Texas counties along the Rio Grande, distributed through Central Power and Light Company and two rural electric cooperatives. The document rejects five alternatives — natural gas, fuel oil, coal, Texas lignite, and nuclear — plus a 'no action' option, because fossil fuels are scarce or polluting, coal and lignite plants run at steady output and cannot efficiently follow peak demand the way hydropower can, and uranium supply is uncertain. The main environmental effects are altered river flows and reservoir levels (Amistad drawn down about 2 feet on average, Falcon raised about 3 feet), and cold, low-oxygen bottom-water releases that could cause minor fish kills in the first 2.2 miles below the dam during July-November. The International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC) held a public meeting in Del Rio on July 1, 1976 where 17 people spoke; the two purchasing cooperatives support the project, while the Fish and Wildlife Service, the City of Eagle Pass, and the downstream Maverick County water district raised concerns about fisheries, drinking-water intakes, and coordinated releases.
